Rasgon, Ph.D. +1 213 559 5917 stacy.rasgon@bernsteinsg.com Nancy Wu +1 917 344 8545 nancy.wu@bernsteinsg.com Quick Take: Meta's will they/won't they neocloud ambitions (situationships don't usually end well) News that Meta is developing plans for a cloud infrastructure business has caused some volatility across the Neocloud and Hardware names. Yet it’s worth noting that at Meta’s AGM at the end of May, Zuckerberg shared that re-selling excess compute was “on the table” if Meta found themselves in an overbuilt situation. At the same time, reports over the weekend point to Google throttling Meta’s compute capacity given their own constraints - curious timing then if Meta is indeed sitting in an overbuild position today. One can absolutely debate the will-they-won’t-they, but we do know that Meta is sitting on one of the largest data center footprints in the world - we estimate \~20GW globally today with another \~14GW coming online in the next few years across its owned and leased portfolio. This scale easily rivals cloud provider footprints. If Meta is developing plans for an externally-facing cloud infrastructure business that could compete head-on with AWS, Azure, GCP… it’s problematic for CoreWeave. We have consistently said that it’s only a matter of time before hyperscalers compete headon with CRWV (see our initiation: Hyperscalers are Situationships, Not Spouses). Meta currently has \$35.2B worth of CRWV contracts, representing a little over a third of CRWV’s backlog. Layer on the \~\$14B from Microsoft, and nearly half of CRWV’s backlog comes from customers who will be full competitors at the time of renewal. We understand that the existing CRWV contracts are tight and difficult to churn out of, so we do not believe there is immediate risk to CRWV’s financials or debt, but we do consider this to be extremely consistent with our thesis: larger, more advantaged competitors will enter the GPUaaS market and CRWV will both lose their existing customers and struggle to compete for new ones. To us, this adds to what we’ve already seen from Google-Blackstone, Colossus, and other fringe players - we anticipate competition will only heat up with time and the CRWV business model will be unsustainable.

There’s a lot of unknowns around Meta’s ambitions worth highlighting:
1. “Developing plans” may not mean launching a competing Neocloud service, though further increases the possibility. And we note the language isn’t far off what Zuckerberg shared at their AGM a month ago. It has already remained an option in case of an overbuild situation. For Meta, even news of developing plans gives investors some semblance of rationality around the cadence and ROIC of the spend, that’s been a major hangup over recent stock performance.
2. Re-selling compute may be temporary until Meta needs it for themselves, especially since Meta is engaged themselves into third-party cloud compute deals with CRWV and GCP. News of Google throttling Meta’s compute needs at the same time could further indicate the importance of keeping excess owned capacity for exactly these moments. Though we note mixed reports on whether the throttling was tied to GCP capacity or specific Gemini usage.
3. The nature of the service could take various forms with very different implications. If Meta chooses to only make Meta’s owned models available via APIs would look very different than a managed multi-model API offering a la Bedrock from AWS and Vertex from GCP. While renting bare metal capacity would be a very different model all together - is it just GPUs or perhaps MTIA as well? All All go-to-market models have very different demand and pricing curves with varying unit economics.
4. If Meta were to enter the Neocloud business, even temporarily, it further raises questions of expected capital to be deployed across the space in 2027 and beyond. Meta remains one of the Big 4 AI check writers in the market today and any change to their spending cadence will likely have dramatic effects across the supply chain.

VALUATION METHODOLOGY
CoreWeave, Inc.
We value CRWV on a forward EV/Adjusted EBIT multiple. Our \$67 price target is based on an Enterprise Value calculated as 28.4x our 2027E Adj. EBIT per share of \$5.81.
Meta Platforms Inc.
We value Meta on a Price Target of \$850 using a 50/50 combination of 2027e EV/Sales multiple of 7x, and a DCF using a WACC of 10% and a terminal growth of 3.5%. We consider Meta primarily a digital advertising business and benchmark valuation to comparable peers in this industry set.
RISKS
CoreWeave, Inc.
The main upside risks to our price target/Underperform rating on CRWV are 1) Delays in hyperscaler built capacity coming online may maintain CRWV value proposition, 2) Development of CRWV’s specialized software platform which maintains demand for CRWV operated data centers, and 3) Continued shortage in power supply to power data centers may sustain CRWV’s pricing power
Meta Platforms Inc.
Downside risk to our target price:
• Meta is currently under investigation in multiple regulatory proceedings now mostly focused on teen-protection and anti-trust domestically and abroad.
• Signs that we’re reaching maturity in digital ads, increased competition as alternatives emerge with compelling ad ROIs, or further privacy related changes (e.g., Cookie depreciation) could all put press on Meta's revenue outlook resulting in compressing revenue growth and de-rating.
• Meta's metaverse aspirations could lead to margin headwinds and potentially minimal ROIC, which could negatively affect both estimates and multiples.
